en: Now, before we dive into horizontal
formatting, let's also talk about this
reading flow again.
Here's another example. It's a JavaScript
file where I call a start function, which
then is defined right below it so that we
can immediately see it.
And that calls a next function, which is
defined right below. And the same is true
for the last function.
Now, if I would execute this file, it would
work and I would log all these log messages.
JavaScript is a language which supports this
syntax. We can call a function before it was
defined because when JavaScript executes, it
automatically pulls all the functions in
front of the other code, so to say.
On the other hand, there are other languages
like Python where this is different.
Here, if we would call start in line 2,
it wouldn't work. This code would fail if we
tried to execute it because in Python we
can't execute a function function before it
was defined.
It will not magically be pulled on top of
the file as it was the case with JavaScript.
So executing start in line 2 wouldn't work.
However, executing it in line 11 here in
this example also wouldn't work. Yes, start
would be defined, but in start I call next
and next at this point of time
when code execution reaches line 11 is still
unknown.
Hence, the only place where we can call
start here is after all these functions have
been defined so that they can call each
other successfully.
So here it's really just about when we start
that function execution, and then Python
simply requires that it saw every function
which is called by some other place in the
code before it's being called.
And therefore, of course, again, you have to
keep such language-specific rules and
restrictions in mind when it comes to
ordering and executing your functions.
